title: It can end
hookLine: the third truth: suffering can cease, what Buddhists call nibbana, a going-out like a flame
carry: a flame that has gone out

lines: THE THIRD TRUTH IS GOOD NEWS.
cards: At the end of a long dinner, somebody leans over and blows out the candle. A thin line of smoke goes up, and then nothing. Where did the flame go?
Not to the kitchen, or out the window. It just isn't burning anymore. The question sounds almost silly, but in the Buddha's teaching it turns out to be a serious one.
The third of his four noble truths is good news, and its word comes from a fire going out.

teach.h: THE THIRD TRUTH: IT CAN END.
teach.b: First, the third truth. In the Buddha's first teaching, after naming suffering and its source, the thirst, he names this: suffering can cease.
It ceases, the text says, with the fading away and ending of that very craving, letting it go, being released from it. Not a new thing added; a thirst that stops. Second, the word.
In Pali it's nibbana; the Sanskrit form is nirvana. The dictionary of the old Pali texts gives its plain sense as the going out of a lamp or a fire. A related word, nibbuta, means cooled, put out.
So the picture isn't a bright new place. It's a fire that has stopped burning, the heat gone out of it.
Third, Patacara's lamp. At the end of her poem in the Therigatha, after watching water run down the slope, she takes a lamp into her room, sits on her bed, and draws out the wick with a needle.
As the lamp goes out, her poem says, her mind was freed: the two in the same moment.

teach.h: WHICH WAY DID THE FIRE GO?
teach.b: Fourth, which way did the fire go? In another teaching, a wanderer named Vacchagotta keeps asking where an awakened one goes after death.
The Buddha asks him back: if a fire in front of you went out, would you know it had gone out? Yes. And which way did it go, east, west, north or south?
The question doesn't fit, says Vacchagotta. A fire that's gone out doesn't go anywhere. The Buddha doesn't answer with a map.
He answers with a flame that has gone out.

how: Buddhists study nibbana as the third noble truth, the ending of craving, and Buddhist schools describe it in different words; meditators practice letting craving cool rather than feeding or forcing it.

o: a deep trance reached only by long hours of sitting
the going out of craving's fire, and with it, suffering
a heavenly realm the awakened travel to after death

games.q: inside the third truth — tap the pairs.
p: drew out the wick, and was freed

s: the texts describe nibbana as a heavenly place you travel to
asked which way a gone-out fire went, Vacchagotta says the question doesn't fit.
the third truth says suffering can cease
with the fading away and ending of craving.
its plain sense is the going out of a lamp or fire.

games.q: you're Vacchagotta. a fire in front of you has gone out. the Buddha asks which way it went: east, west, north or south?
o: the question doesn't fit: it went nowhere
games.why: Vacchagotta himself says the question doesn't fit, and the Buddha uses the fire to answer his question about the awakened.

practice: Find one craving burning a little right now, for praise, for quiet, for an apology, for this to be over, and picture it as a small lamp flame.

Patacara didn't blow hers out; she drew the wick down, so on each out-breath let the wick of this wanting sink a little lower, no snuffing, no fanning. It may not go out; see if it cools, even a little.

wordCard.voice: Nibbana: Pali, in Sanskrit nirvana, the going out of a fire. In the third noble truth, the ending of craving, and with it, suffering. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: the going out of a fire. The Sanskrit form is nirvāṇa.

carryVoice: Your line: a flame that has gone out. The third truth is the good news: it can end. Day seven hundred six.
